articles.title_orig: World Athletics referee and race walking judge Costin's steps to success
articles.title_zh: World Athletics referee and race walking judge Costin's steps to success
articles.content_orig:
Zuzana Costin at the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26 ( © World Athletics Media Academy Lenny Patram Jr. )
Zuzana Costin is a former athlete turned official, currently the only active female technical official in the world to hold both World Athletics Gold Level Referee and Gold Level Race Walking Judge qualifications.
The two-time Olympian, who competed in the 20km race walk at the Athens 2004 and Beijing 2008 Games, most recently served as a race walking judge and referee during the World Athletics U20 Championships Oregon 26. While there, she reflected on her journey in athletics.
You hold both World Athletics Gold Level Referee and Gold Level Race Walking Judge qualifications – currently the only active female technical official in the world to do so. What does this achievement mean to you?
"There are three of us who hold both qualifications but, yes, I am the only female official. It’s quite amazing to have achieved this. I always try to do the best that I can, therefore it’s nice to see that the work I have put in was recognised, and it paid off."
When you first began your journey as a technical official, did you ever imagine you would reach this level?
"No, I didn’t. I got involved in athletics at a very young age. My dad (Jozef Malik) was the Vice President of the federation (Slovak Athletic Federation) for several years and was active as an administrator, coach and also as an official, so I grew up in the world of athletics. Any time he organised any competitions, I was helping out. So it has always been a part of my life and I never thought about it too much at that stage. Achieving this level in officiating in athletics after finishing my racing career gives me a strong sense of accomplishment and satisfaction."
Throughout your career, have there been mentors who helped shape your journey?
"Undeniably, my dad played a big role at the beginning of my journey and he has kept supporting me since.
"After retiring from being an athlete, I started to officiate in Ireland on a regular basis (I had moved there a few years beforehand). I met with support and encouragement to pursue this to an international level. I was very lucky that I was immersed in an environment where people knew what they were doing, not just on a local level but on an international one, too. So, whenever I came across any problems, I had people I could rely on.
"After passing the Silver level exam, I started getting appointments at European competitions and there were always senior technical officials who were happy to share their knowledge and experience with ‘newbies’.
"That was also the case during one of my first big international appointments as a member of the Jury of Appeal at the European Championships in Berlin where Anna Riccardi was our chief. She took me under her wing, gave me confidence and guided me through this new experience.
"During the Covid-19 pandemic, European Athletics began organising online webinars for technical officials, focusing heavily on the practical aspects of officiating. Those webinars were primary led by Chris Cohen and Niels van der Aar and they helped me to become a more knowledgeable and effective official.
"Later, I was selected for the European Athletics mentoring programme for technical delegates and was appointed as a mentee technical delegate for the European Championships in Rome. I was fortunate to have Chris and Niels as my mentors; their guidance provided invaluable insights and allowed me to expand my knowledge even further."
What practical support is most beneficial for upcoming female officials during the early stages of their careers?
"Having someone you can turn to, talk to and learn from is major. Mentorship is something you can’t replace, especially when you are trying to excel.
"After World Athletics changed its educational programme for officials to the current one, it really opened the door for younger people. Originally, the educational programme and exams to become an international official were only in English, which could be a bit of a barrier for people who don’t have a good standard of English. That is still the case for the Gold level. And this could be something that a mentor could help with – dismantling the language barrier. However, for the lower levels, World Athletics has gradually introduced more languages in which its certification courses and exams can be taken. This shift definitely benefits new candidates who don’t have a sufficient command of English."
Since you started your career, have you seen an increase in more female judges, applicants or volunteers for athletics?
"Absolutely. I don’t remember seeing many female officials in the leading positions when I started, and that has definitely changed now. Also, World Athletics’ encouragement to member federations to enter an equal number of female and male candidates for exams has started to pay off. Panels of international officials are now nearly gender balanced.
"I have also seen a growth in the numbers of younger officials, with more opportunities and positions available for them. It’s more achievable and something that one can work towards now."
What kind of advice would you give someone, especially a younger woman, who is interested in following your footsteps or becoming a judge in athletics?
"Now is the right time. Ask your federation about upcoming courses and exams. If you get opportunities to take part in them or you get any appointments, don’t turn them down because you can always learn something. You might not succeed all the time, but you learn from the experience.
"It is also important to believe in yourself and to have someone, or a group of people, that you can get support from.
"It is nice to see new candidates growing in confidence. When they first get started, it’s all very nerve-racking and there’s so much going on all at once – it creates a lot of feelings of fear. But that’s a normal thing to experience. Sometimes all they need is someone in their corner telling them that this is normal, to believe in themselves, and that someone else has confidence in them."
What kind of legacy do you hope to leave – not only through the competitions you’ve officiated, but through the people you’ve inspired?
"I just hope that all the younger officials coming in see that they can do this. That this, as well as whatever else they want to strive for, is achievable regardless of whether they are coming from a country with a strong tradition of international officiating or not. And that the journey of being an international official can start at any age."
Ash Wehrly for the World Athletics Media Academy
Launched in March, the World Athletics pledge initiative forms part of the organisation’s contribution to the International Women’s Day 2026 global campaign, #GiveToGain, which calls on individuals and organisations to give their time, resources and support to help forge gender equality through abundant giving. By encouraging stakeholders to pledge mentoring hours, World Athletics is turning the #GiveToGain message into practical action across the sport. Learn more on the Women in Athletics website .

articles.title_orig: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.title_zh: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.content_orig:
For scientists searching for life beyond Earth, rocky planets with atmospheres are among the most promising places to investigate. An atmosphere is essential for maintaining liquid water on a planet's surface. Yet among the more than 6,300 exoplanets cataloged thus far, most are not rocky, and only a small number of known rocky planets appear to possess atmospheres.
Now, researchers have added another world to that short list. In a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , a team led by University of Chicago scientist Brandon Park Coy reports evidence of an atmosphere surrounding HD 3167 b, a rocky super-Earth located 154 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. The intensely hot planet, classified as a "lava world," completes an orbit around its star in only one Earth day.
"What's so surprising is that the closer a rocky planet orbits its star, the harder it should be to have an atmosphere, because it's bombarded by stellar wind and gets more high-energy photons from the star. But it seems that many of these lava worlds do," explained Edwin Kite, UChicago associate professor of geophysical sciences and co-author of the study. "These planets are too hot for life, but by studying them, we can say something about the processes that matter for other rocky worlds."
In the Q&A below,Coy, a graduate student in Kite's group and first author on the study, explains why atmospheres on lava worlds are scientifically valuable, how researchers detected evidence for this one, and what they hope to learn next.
What was the goal of the survey that found this atmosphere-bearing exoplanet?
One of the driving questions that the James Webb Space Telescope is being used to answer is whether planets orbiting stars much smaller than the sun have atmospheres. It appears that most of those terrestrial planets don't -- they're just bare rock.
But surprisingly, we've found evidence that the majority of lava worlds -- similar in composition to Earth and Venus but much, much hotter -- might have atmospheres. Five terrestrial planets found with atmospheres, including the one described in this study, have been ultra-hot.
This planet, however, is the coldest lava world found so far with evidence of an atmosphere. This is interesting because we're trying to understand the temperature transition between planets with and without atmospheres.
The result is the first from a program led by Megan Weiner Mansfield, PhD'21, who's now at the University of Maryland. The goal of the program, which is looking at 10 ultra-hot lava worlds, is to see if there's a critical temperature over which you start seeing planets with atmospheres.
"We're interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world." -- Study author Brandon Park Coy
How can you tell if an exoplanet has an atmosphere?
Right now, directly looking at Earth-like planets for signs of life is out of reach. Instead, we can use the Webb telescope to detect light in the mid-infrared wavelength range to estimate the temperature of exoplanets, which can tell us if they might have atmospheres.
There are two primary ways that we study exoplanets. One is called transit, when the planet goes in front of the host star. Another called secondary eclipse, which is the method we used for this study, is when the planet passes behind its star, and we can measure how much light is lost. That difference tells us how much mid-infrared light comes from the planet itself, which essentially tells us how hot the planet is.
If a planet doesn't have an atmosphere, its star-facing, day side should be as hot as theoretically possible based on how reflective its surface is and its distance from the star. But an atmosphere would help redistribute heat from the day side to the night side. We see this happen on Venus -- there's almost no difference in surface temperature between the day and night sides, or between the poles and the equator. If a planet has an atmosphere, it might also have clouds that reflect incoming starlight and cool the dayside. So if a planet's day side is cooler than the maximum possible, it likely has an atmosphere.
The subject of this study, HD 3167 b, is noticeably cooler than its expected maximum, providing strong evidence that it has an atmosphere.
What do you think HD 3167 b's atmosphere is made of?
These lava worlds are so-named because the surface facing their star is likely melted rock. We think that HD 3167 b might have a silicate-rich composition, with a similar mixture of minerals that make up Earth's mantle. Before this study, we expected that any atmosphere on these ultra-hot planets would be composed of vaporized rock, but we're starting to see evidence that some might have heavier gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, or water in their atmospheres.
The makeup of HD 3167 b's atmosphere is still up in the air. That's one reason we're so interested in getting new observations.
Why is this result important?
Because the four other lava worlds found to have atmospheres are in the ultra-hot regime, it raises questions about whether there's a critical transition temperature when silicate atmospheres start becoming very thick. Is there a temperature where these planets form silicate cloud decks that might reflect incoming radiation to space and cool its day side? This relatively cooler planet helps us better characterize and nail down this transition.
Despite how inhospitable they are for life, we're also interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world. We think that very early in the solar system's history, when the terrestrial planets formed, they were extremely hot due to the energy from all of the planetesimal collisions. Earth had what's known as a magma ocean stage with an entirely liquid surface. This result gives us a window into studying what conditions may have been like in Earth's first couple of million years.

articles.title_orig: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.title_zh: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This CNN Travel series is, or was, sponsored by the country it highlights. CNN retains full editorial control over subject matter, reporting and frequency of the articles and videos within the sponsorship, in compliance with our policy .
Standing at the crossroad of continents, Istanbul has long been a global linchpin.
As Byzantium and then Constantinople, it controlled trade routes along the Silk Road and maritime passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean.
In the golden age of railways, Istanbul was the end point of the Orient Express, at the very cusp of Europe and Asia.
Now, in the 21st century, iGA Istanbul Airport is ruling the skies, having just overtaken London Heathrow as the best-connected airport on the planet.
“They’ve finally got the number one position,” says John Grant, chief analyst at OAG, a global travel data provider which has just released its Megahubs 2026 Index, comparing the world’s top airports.
The rankings are generated by comparing the number of scheduled connections to and from international flights , with the number of destinations served from the airport. They do this through a snapshot look at the busiest day of the year, which this year was August 2.
Gaining the top spot is “an important achievement for iGA Istanbul Airport and reflects the position we have built as a global aviation hub,” airport CEO Selahattin Bilgen tells CNN. “Today, we already serve approximately 350 destinations around the world, with significant room to grow further.”
Amsterdam Airport Schiphol is third place in this year’s ranking, followed by Kuala Lumpur at No.4 and Chicago O’Hare at No.5.
It’s been a swift and impressive rise for the award-winning $12 billion Istanbul Airport, which opened to much fanfare in 2018, about 20 miles outside Istanbul on the European side. This is a hub built for scale: Its huge 1.4-million-square-meter terminal is the world’s largest under one roof and the whole 76.5-million-square-meter site is bigger than Manhattan.
More than 84 million passengers pass through each year, making it the eighth busiest airport in the world. However, the long-term plan is to increase capacity to 200 million passengers per year, which is double the annual number currently handled by Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta, the world’s busiest airport.
“They’re going to be unassailable in the coming years,” says Grant. “They’ve got runway capacity. They’ve got a national airline that is hugely successful and continues to grow with new fleet orders. They’re very close to some of the most emergent markets in the world, such as Central Asia. They’ve benefited partly from the Middle East situation. They’re just very well placed.”
Istanbul Airport opened its fourth main runway last month and the end goal is for the hub to have nine: six main and three reserve.
The new  2,820-meter-long runway is its first to run east to west, meaning a reduction in taxiing and airborne times for westbound aircraft, saving time and fuel.
“They’re the only airport in the world that is licensed for three simultaneous runway operations,” says Grant, “You can build more frequency at those peak hours, and it gives you more operational flexibility. If you’ve got three runways, then you’re likely to improve your punctuality.”
Secrets of the sultan’s palace where concubines and eunuchs lived
Turkish Airlines has an 80% share of flights at Istanbul Airport and plays a key role in the hub’s success. Two years ago, it entered Guinness World Records for its achievement in flying to more countries than any other airline: 130 in total, as of 2026.
It operates a modern and rapidly expanding fleet of more than 500 Boeing and Airbus aircraft, including a diverse mix of narrow and widebody planes.
A younger fleet makes “a better impression” on customers, says Viktoriia Myroniuk, a senior lecturer in air transport management at the UK’s Cranfield University, reflecting on the polished service that helped earn Turkish Airlines its recent Skytrax award for Best Airline in Europe .
Newer aircraft are also more efficient, which, in this time of rising fuel prices, gives the airline a competitive edge, allowing them to lower ticket prices.
Selahattin Bilgen, CEO of iGA Istanbul Airport, tells CNN, “The efficiency and cost advantages we provide continue to attract new airlines to our network each year, and today we are one of only two major hubs worldwide serving the largest number of airlines.”
Infrastructure is equally key to that connectivity. “As a relatively new airport, iGA İstanbul Airport was designed from the outset with growth in mind, providing the capacity and flexibility to accommodate increasing passenger demand and support our role as a major international transfer hub.”
OAG’s 2026 Megahub rankings are inevitably affected by the ongoing disruption in the Middle East, as well as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
While other airports and regions have suffered, Istanbul Airport and Turkey’s geographical position and diplomatic relations have by chance granted it better fortune.
Istanbul Airport has the flexibility and capacity for growth that its competitors in the region lack. London Heathrow’s plan for a third runway remains highly controversial, due to the environmental impact in a highly built-up corner of southeast England. Amsterdam Schiphol, the world’s third best connected, has a flight cap of 488,000 movements a year.
“The fact that Istanbul Airport is slightly on the outskirts” means “they can operate 24/7,” says Myroniuk.
She also praises Turkish Airlines’ stopover program , which allows connecting passengers to take a break to explore Istanbul and enjoy free accommodation in partner hotels.
“I’m one of those unlucky passengers who really can’t sleep on board” and struggle on economy flights, Myroniuk says, but “your luggage stays with Turkish Airlines. You go to the perfect night’s rest.”
She married her brother, then he died. The monument to her grief was a Wonder of the Ancient World
It’s a form of sustainable tourism, she says, allowing travelers to embrace slower travel and to connect with local culture, rather than notching up cheap connecting flights with no experiences to show for it.
For many passengers it is also easier to get a visa to stop off in Turkey than it would be to take an exploratory tour from an EU airport, so that’s another advantage Istanbul Airport enjoys.
Although it’s hard to make any predictions in these turbulent times, Grant says that “all things being equal,” Istanbul will continue to hold onto its position in 2027.
“I think we’re going to see over the next three or four years the Chinese airports strengthen in their positions. We’re seeing more international growth from Chinese airlines, and that will help them,” he says.
International airlines including British Airways have yet to resume flying to the Middle East, but airports in the region will hopefully “get back to where they were,” says Grant. “All of which will continue to chip away at the position at Heathrow and Amsterdam Schiphol, and Paris, where we have European airports” that are reaching capacity.

articles.title_orig: Experimental vaccine shows promise against deadly brain cancer in some patients
articles.title_zh: Experimental vaccine shows promise against deadly brain cancer in some patients
articles.content_orig:
MimiVax's cancer vaccine missed the primary endpoint of a phase 2 study in patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma, although the biotech suggested the results among under-65s still offer a path forward for the candidate.
The New York-based company evaluated the peptide-mimic immunotherapeutic vaccine, called SurVaxM, against placebo in 233 evaluable patients with newly diagnosed brain cancer. SurVaxM was tied to a median overall survival (OS) of 24.2 months compared to 20.2 months for the placebo cohort.
While MimiVax claimed this improvement was “clinically meaningful,” the company admitted in an Oct. 7 release that the result missed the study's primary endpoint.
The biotech homed in on a prespecified subset of patients aged 65 years and younger. Among this subgroup, the OS difference was 24.2 months and 20.2 months, which MimiVax described as a “significant benefit.”
This subset of patients also saw an improvement in progression-free survival at 12 months, with 44% of those who received SurVaxM reaching this mark compared to 24% on placebo. A long-term survival analysis showed that approximately 42% of SurVaxM-treated patients 65 and under were alive through 30 months or longer, with no further deaths reported up to 54 months.
Despite the topline fail, MimiVax said these subgroup findings still give the company the confidence to pursue a path toward potential FDA approval for SurVaxM.
“Even very small increases in survival are very significant to the patients, taking into perspective that there hasn't been a new GBM drug in over 20 years,” MimiVax CEO Michael Ciesielski, Ph.D., told Fierce.
“There are really no options for these patients,” he added. “There's nothing else to offer them, so any improvement is significant.”
Glioblastoma is the most common and aggressive brain tumor in adults. After diagnosis, patients typically succumb to the tumor within about 18 months, despite standard-of-care therapy. These tumors have multiple mechanisms for skirting treatment, making them notably hard to treat, with no advances since the addition of the chemotherapy agent temozolomide in 2005 .
“There just hasn't been anything in such a long time for these patients, and there's been so many failed trials in between,” Ciesielski said. “It's inspiring to finally see something start to move the needle against this disease.”
SurVaxM is engineered against survivin, a protein that stymies programmed cell death and can make tumor cells resistant to standard treatments. The cancer vaccine aims to train the immune system to recognize survivin-expressing cells and respond to them, as the protein is highly expressed in nearly 95% of GBM tumors and many other cancers, Ciesielski noted.
“We wanted to target something that was highly expressed and accessible to the immune system—this fit the bill,” the CEO explained.
The phase 2b study built on an open-label phase 2a trial that concluded in 2022, where patients treated with SurVaxM alongside adjuvant temozolomide showed a median OS of 25.9 months.
Patients received four primary injections of SurVaxM—one dose every two weeks for four doses, followed by a booster injection every two months—after undergoing standard-of-care therapy that included maximum tumor resection, chemo and radiotherapy.
When it came to safety, adverse events being mainly Grade 1 and 2 injection site reactions. Grade 3 or higher adverse events were seen in 48% of patients treated with SurVaxM versus 46% with placebo.
MimiVax spun out of the Roswell Park Comprehensive Cancer Center in Buffalo, New York in 2012. Besides SurVaxM, the biotech is currently running multiple mid-stage trials testing its cancer vaccines in metastatic neuroendocrine tumors and multiple myeloma, and it plans to open a study soon for preventative lung cancer.
Other companies have joined MimiVax in trying to find a fresh approach to treating glioblastoma—with mixed results. Imvax's phase 2b study of its autologous cell immunotherapy and device combination product flunked a phase 2b study at the end of last year. Meanwhile, Evaxion is prioritizing glioblastoma for its off-the-shelf therapeutic vaccine in collaboration with Duke University, while BrainChild Bio is attacking pediatric brain cancer with its triple-targeting CAR T-cell therapy that is expected to enter the clinic next year.

On 25 September 2026, World Lung Day highlighted the importance of respiratory health as a public health priority, calling for stronger prevention, earlier detection, equitable access to care and healthier environments.
Respiratory diseases remain a major public health challenge across Europe. While many lung diseases are preventable, addressing their impact requires coordinated action from policymakers, healthcare professionals, researchers and communities.
This year’s message, “Healthy Lungs, Healthy Populations,” emphasised the need to translate scientific evidence into effective public health action.
These priorities closely align with the objectives of the Joint Action on Respiratory Diseases (JARED), which brings together European partners to improve respiratory health, strengthen prevention and reduce health inequalities.
World Lung Day serves as a reminder that protecting lung health requires sustained commitment and collaboration across sectors.

articles.title_orig: As measles rages, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe
articles.title_zh: As measles rages, one clinic leans on years of hard-won trust to keep vulnerable people safe
articles.content_orig:
Main Street is bustling on a Wednesday afternoon in late September. Cars mix with horse-and-buggy carriages on the road, many coming and going from the weekly Sale Day — a market spread over 10 acres with livestock, fruits and vegetables, flowers and other goods for available to purchase. Lively conversations in English and Pennsylvania Dutch fill the barn where a produce auction stretches until lunchtime; bids for a pint of bright red cherry tomatoes run from 90 cents to $1.30.
As dozens of people mix and mingle through the afternoon — Amish and other Plain people, so named for their simple way of dressing, as well as “English,” as they refer to folks outside of their community — there are no direct indications that a measles outbreak is raging in the area. Only one woman has a mask on, which she says she’s been wearing any time she’s left home since the start of the Covid-19 pandemic. One vendor is closed for “unexpected family obligations,” and one regular auction attendee is mourned after her recent sudden death after having “flu-like symptoms.” Tourists are visiting from Brooklyn.
But less than a mile away at the Central Pennsylvania Clinic, measles is front and center.
A turn off of Main Street quickly opens up to an idyllic rural valley, filled with lush farms set to a backdrop of rolling green mountains. An unlined road leads across a babbling river to reveal a striking gray building up on a hill, a massive barn raised in the traditional style that uses only wood pegs — no nails — to hold the structure together.
The front door is locked, with a photo and description of measles hanging in the window, along with a notice asking visitors to “ring doorbell for service.” Dr. Katherine Mascia swings the door open with a big smile and a quick question: “Any measles symptoms today?”
Beneath the genuine smile is true heartbreak. A massive measles outbreak in the area — as of Wednesday, the largest and deadliest the United States has had in decades — is bringing significant pain and suffering to the families she cares for.
“In the five years that I’ve worked here, I don’t think we’ve had so many patients admitted to the hospital all within the span of a few weeks,” Mascia said. “We might usually have maybe one patient who’s admitted for their complex care needs, but to have so many all at the same time, it’s really unprecedented.”
More than 1,000 measles cases have been reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health since the outbreak started in April, surpassing recent record-breaking outbreaks – in Texas and South Carolina last year – to become the worst in the US since the early 1990s. The clinic’s home of Mifflin County is one the hardest-hit, near the epicenter in neighboring Lancaster County.
The patients who the Central Pennsylvania Clinic serves are especially vulnerable to the severe effects of a measles infection. The nonprofit is centered around caring for children and adults with genetic disorders that are especially common among the Amish and broader Plain community, a group that also tends to have lower vaccination rates than average.
The Plain people are known for their ​caution toward government and other nonreligious authority.
But as measles tears through many of their hometowns in central Pennsylvania, the national conversation has become paradoxically politically charged.
Leaders from the federal government and the Pennsylvania government have clashed over the response , with much of the debate centered around the five deaths that have come during this outbreak. Disputes over the definition of what counts as a measles death and how news of the deaths is shared with the public have disrupted public health response plans.
Meanwhile, the Central Pennsylvania Clinic’s staff is focused on how to best keep everyone safe and healthy. They’re leaning on the clinic’s well-forged foundation of trust. It has taken persistence and patience — sometimes years — for the clinic to build those relationships, and the strength of that trust has faced some of its greatest tests over the past few months.
When Pennsylvania reported a measles-associated death in an 18-year-old in Mifflin County, Mascia said, the clinic started to get tons of calls — from patients they knew and other members of the broader community — who just wanted to know what happened. They weren’t paying attention to what government officials were arguing about on social media, she said. They wanted a clear understanding of how the young person died.
“I’m quite honored that they’re calling us and asking those questions. It helps me feel like they really trust us,” Mascia said. “But it puts pressure on us, too.”
She said she reached out to the county coroner directly to get a formal statement on the cause of death, and she references that statement when patients have questions.
“We want to keep that line of communication open with the community, and it’s so important to provide accurate information and be consistent with the messaging,” she said.
Central Pennsylvania Clinic leaders have been thinking about and planning for a measles outbreak in the community since the start of the West Texas outbreak in January 2025, Mascia said. Their patients are vulnerable, and their offices, while incredibly well-equipped in many ways, are not built to treat measles patients.
“We don’t have advanced ventilation systems, and we don’t have negative-pressure rooms, so if a person who is infected with measles comes in, our entire building is compromised for two hours,” Mascia said.
Pennsylvania requires a throat swab, a blood sample and a urine sample to confirm a measles case — arduous tasks for both ill patients, who often had to take a taxing horse and buggy ride to the clinic, and for clinic staff who have to work within the constraints of their facility.
The rear entrance to the clinic building, which also hosts a federally qualified health center, has become a makeshift triage center for people with suspected measles cases. The back parking lot is large enough for cars and buggies to spread out, and clinic staffers meet families at the door, where they can lead the patient into a small storage barn to collect urine samples.
It was important to have a logistical plan to keep operations safe, Mascia said, but she pointedly explains that the most critical way to protect their patients is to raise vaccination rates.
The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely effective. One dose is 93% effective against measles, and the recommended second dose bumps that protection up to 97% — and the immunity is lifelong. Extensive research has also demonstrated the vaccine’s safety .
Childhood vaccination rates have been falling nationwide, with a record share of parents opting to exempt their new kindergartners from the required shots last school year.
Vaccination rates tend to be lower among Plain people, but it’s not because of an inherent opposition, experts say.
There are certain shared values within the community, but there are also varied individual beliefs and opinions about vaccines, as there would in any broad group of people, Mascia said. Consistency in the clinic’s messaging around vaccination has been the key to raising coverage rates.
If the patients sense any type of coercion from doctors or if they feel forced into a decision about something like a vaccination, they’ll completely disengage from all health care – an outcome that would be particularly troublesome for the vulnerable patients they care for.
“We share that it’s our strong recommendation that everyone be fully vaccinated,” Mascia said. “And if they’re not interested, we repeat our recommendation and say ‘we’re here to help if and when you change your mind.’”

articles.title_orig: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
articles.title_zh: An early flu season means it might be time to think about a flu shot
articles.content_orig:
An early start to the flu season means it might be time to consider a flu shot. Rebecca Blackwell/AP hide caption
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Fall has only just begun, but it's already time to start thinking about the quintessential winter bug: the flu .
The annual flu season usually starts in October or November. But this year, it looks like the flu started to pick up in early September.
"There are enough signs pointing in the same direction to make me think, 'OK, yes. This is the start of flu season,'" says Caitlin Rivers , an epidemiologist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
The percentage of people testing positive for the flu in the West has been rising steadily since around the beginning of September, she says. And the number of people showing up in emergency departments because of the flu has also been rising for weeks, she adds.
"It's very uncommon to see flu activity rising this early. It's activity that we might normally see more like November or December," she says.
The timing of the flu season isn't the only thing that's odd. It's also unusual that flu activity seems to have started in Western states, such as California, Washington, Hawaii and Alaska.
"It typically starts in the South and then expands from there," Rivers says. "So two uncommon developments there."
Rivers stresses that the amount of flu activity is still very low in most parts of the country. But that's starting to change as the flu picks up nationwide.
It's unclear why flu activity would have started so early, and in such an unusual part of the country. But one clue might be a new variant that evolved a mutation, which appears to make it better at evading existing immunity, especially among teenagers.
"That's our best argument for what's going on right now in terms of this early flu season," says Dr. Alex Greninger , a virologist who heads infectious disease diagnostics at the University of Washington. Doctors there are seeing as much flu right now as they usually would around Christmas, and the mutated variant appears to be common, he says.
So Greninger, Rivers and others are urging people to think about getting their flu shot earlier than usual.
"It's crucial that people get an influenza vaccine," says Scott Hensley , a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania. "And this might be a year that people might want to get a vaccine early."
But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn't been promoting flu shots as it usually does. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who oversees the CDC, is a long-time vaccine skeptic.
"It is disappointing that CDC is quiet given that flu kills of hundreds of kids a year and can result in tens of thousands of hospitalizations and tens of thousands of deaths," says Dr. Demetre Daskalakis , who resigned last year as the director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to protest what he called political interference at the agency.
The CDC declined to make an official available to NPR for this story. In a statement, a CDC spokesperson said, "CDC is developing a communications strategy to provide clear, accessible information about influenza vaccination and other critical steps people can take to protect themselves during respiratory virus season. This includes information about the benefits and risks of vaccination to support informed decision-making."

articles.title_orig: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.title_zh: Why AI is both the hope and the hazard for world leaders, according to IMF chief Georgieva
articles.content_orig:
SINGAPORE — The technology that investors and governments are counting on to lift the global economy is also adding pressure that threatens growth, the head of the International Monetary Fund said, urging policymakers to stop delaying painful choices on debt.
Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva told the audience at a Wednesday event in Singapore that artificial intelligence is "rapidly becoming a key driver of countries' relative fortunes in the world economy."
But the triple forces of AI advancement, soaring energy costs and record public debt are challenging the already "underwhelming" growth this decade.
"Love it, hate it, or fear it, AI is here," Georgieva said.
Speaking ahead of a series of IMF and World Bank annual meetings that kick off next week, Georgieva framed the global economy as being tugged in two directions at once: a "negative energy supply shock" from the war in the Gulf, now in its eighth month, and a "positive demand shock" from the AI investment boom. The combined effect, she said, is "highly uneven across the world."
On the upside, global AI investment as a share of GDP will reach, and likely exceed, the amounts that went into building the railroads, electricity grid, or telecommunications network. AI hardware and related technology products already account for more than a tenth of world goods trade, she said.
The IMF estimates that AI could add up to half a percentage point to annual world growth if done right. "Going from 3% to 3.5% over a decade — that is like adding an economy the size of ASEAN to the world economy," Georgieva said.
But the benefits are likely highly concentrated. The boom largely bypasses economies less involved in the global AI supply chain, "increasing the risk of widening economic inequality across the globe," she said.
The boom also feeds the inflation worry that has dogged policymakers from the U.S. to Europe and Asia. "The AI building boom is inflationary," she said, as are energy and food shocks, tariffs and defense spending.
Oil prices have stayed above $100 per barrel as the Middle East conflict dragged on with few signs of a diplomatic off-ramp. Retail diesel prices also rose to record highs as refining capacity squeezed energy supplies.
That inflation pressure flows straight into bond markets, as bond yields in the U.S., Germany, and Japan have surged to their highest levels in decades . Ballooning long-term private bond issuance by AI-related borrowers also competes with governments for capital, although part of the rise may reflect expectations of faster growth, Georgieva said.
Global public debt is near its highest level since World War II and on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP, with advanced economies the "worst offenders," Georgieva said. For 17 years, governments had "a relatively easy ride" because interest rates stayed below growth rates. "Higher interest rates now put an end to that."
The interest-to-growth differential is now "much less favourable" and "set to climb higher," she said, which means the growth needed to reduce debt ratios without fiscal effort is now "out of reach in the near term."
The strain is already visible in Europe, where spreads over German bunds are widening not just for France and Italy but for Ireland, Portugal and others that had reduced debt and deficits after the euro-area crisis.
After a string of shocks that have ballooned public debt and most countries' fiscal deficits remained above pre-pandemic averages, "fiscal space is crying out for replenishment," Georgieva said.
Georgieva also pointed to a financial stability risk in the AI boom itself. Strong corporate earnings are driving share prices and wealth effects, she said, but "should earnings fall short, however, hyperscaler leverage and large and growing global holdings of U.S. equities could turn a disappointment into a far-reaching shock."
Citing Amara's Law, which holds that people overestimate a new technology in the short run and underestimate it in the long run, she said it is "somewhere in the transition between today's AI building boom and tomorrow's arrival of AI's benefits that we will traverse the period of maximum risk."
Georgieva said the first line of defense is regulation and supervision. "Now may be a good time for a prudently hawkish bias in many countries' monetary policy," she said.

articles.title_orig: Cornell officials pressed by faculty as outrage mounts over alleged gang rape
articles.title_zh: Cornell officials pressed by faculty as outrage mounts over alleged gang rape
articles.content_orig:
Gang rape allegations at Cornell University are fueling a firestorm of actions against the school, against fraternity members named in a lawsuit and against the former student known as Jane Doe, whose accusations have galvanized a nationwide reckoning of sexual assault on college campuses .
Doe, who recently filed a lawsuit alleging gang rape at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024, has now received death threats, her attorney Thomas Giuffra said. He provided CNN audio of one of the harassing calls.
Doe was also targeted in a swatting incident , during which police drew guns on her family and a friend, the attorney told CNN’s Jake Tapper.
“The temperature needs to be brought down,” Giuffra said, blaming the threats on commentators who have doxxed the woman and accused her of lying. “I am very concerned for her and her family’s safety.”
A timeline of the Cornell gang rape allegations
Meanwhile, some of the accused fraternity members – and even others who are unrelated to the case but have the same names – have faced public backlash as the investigation unfolds.
And Cornell, which recently announced a former Justice Department official will investigate the school’s handling of sexual assault claims, is the site of a seven-hour sit-in on campus to show “solidarity with Jane Doe,” according to flyers for the event.
Sexual assault survivor says Cornell Jane Doe is ‘not alone’, and laments lack of accountability
The state attorney general has launched a separate investigation as questions mount over how Cornell police handled Jane Doe’s allegations, how much information was shared with the district attorney’s office at the time, why prosecutors initially decided not to file charges , and whether the school’s internal investigation and actions went far enough.
Professors joined students at a rally this week, where demonstrators held signs reading “Justice for every Jane Doe” and “Cornell admin betrays survivors resign now.”
While Cornell’s president expressed his own anger about what happened with Jane Doe’s case, at least one faculty member is now calling for his resignation.
Some accused students are still in school: University officials confirmed two students named in Doe’s civil lawsuit last month are still enrolled and attending classes, according to a recording of a virtual webinar obtained by CNN. Some faculty members said they’re struggling to teach classes the accused students are in and raised questions about how to accommodate them and other students.
Faculty member calls for president’s resignation: “There are layers of concerns that need to be addressed. And I think the only way to begin that process is to see resignations and a turnover in our upper administration,” Cornell Faculty Senate member Ariana Kim told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer on Wednesday morning. She specifically called for the resignation of Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff, who was interim president at the time of Doe’s allegations to campus police in 2024.
Doe’s attorney details more threats: Doe has been targeted with threats and attempts to publicize her identity, her attorney told CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Tuesday night. “Just before I got on with you, somebody called her, made a threat to shoot up her house, shoot her, her mother, her father. She’s calling the police as we speak now,” Giuffra told Cooper. While Doe has received other threats since filing her lawsuit, this was the first phone call, Giuffra said. “We’re terrified,” said the attorney, who previously said that he himself received a threat Sunday morning.
Jane Doe receives phone threat over Cornell case, attorney says
Mayor calls for a pause on student gatherings : The Ithaca Common Council is scheduled to meet at 6 p.m. Wednesday at City Hall as Mayor Robert Cantelmo seeks council action on a proposed moratorium on student and special event permits – including Greek life and other student gatherings – following the allegations of gang rape at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024.
No-confidence vote coming: The Faculty Senate will review a resolution for a no-confidence vote before it’s added to the Senate’s meeting agenda for October 14, labor history professor and Faculty Senate member Paul Ortiz said. The Senate is Cornell’s main legislative advisory and review body, with more than 75 members representing the university’s faculty. So far, about 40 senators have supported a resolution to hold a vote of no confidence, Ortiz said. CNN has reached out to Cornell officials for comment.
Cornell says ex-US Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates will investigate school’s response to Jane Doe’s rape allegations
Students host town hall : Students on Tuesday also hosted a town hall to discuss the ongoing issues on campus. A young woman in attendance said the event had helped “restore my faith in the community.” Another student said they were glad to see the media spotlight being shined on the school. “Sexual violence should make the headlines. It should be shocking, it should be newsworthy because it should be incredibly rare,” they said.
Cornell announces independent review : Former US Deputy Attorney General Sally Q. Yates will lead an independent review of how Cornell University “prevents and responds to sexual harassment, sexual assault and related misconduct on campus,” the university announced Tuesday. Yates and her team will “conduct a detailed review of the university’s response” to Doe’s allegations, “including whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to the matter,” the university said.
The cycle of denial and shame felt by Cornell’s Jane Doe follows a typical pattern for sexual assault survivors, experts say
Sexual violence survivors reach out for help in near-record numbers : Over the past week, calls to the National Sexual Assault Hotline are up 73%, and there were more than double the normal number of calls on Monday alone, according to the Rape, Abuse and Incest National Network, which operates the hotline. Many of those contacting the hotline said reading about Doe’s case inspired them to call, RAINN President Scott Berkowitz said. “We admire – and are so grateful for – Jane Doe’s courage,” Berkowitz said. “RAINN stands with her, as do millions of survivors and supporters across the country.”
Cornell police tried to get phone records in Jane Doe’s sex assault investigation. Her lawyer says records never got to DA
Cornell police drafted requests to phone companies : Documents reveal Cornell police drafted letters to wireless carriers while “investigating a sexual assault incident” about a week after Doe first reported the alleged assault to university police. The drafts, addressed to Verizon and T-Mobile, asked them to “preserve all available data,” including texts, calls, and picture and video messages associated with accounts that “may contain evidence pertinent to the ongoing investigation.” It’s not clear whether investigators ever sent those requests or followed up with subpoenas. And it’s also unclear whether Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten was aware of the 2024 draft letters. The DA has said Cornell police only gave his office a six-page statement signed by Doe and Snapchat screenshots in 2024. CNN has asked the carriers whether they received the requests from Cornell and if they complied.
Prosecutors refused additional evidence : The Tompkins County District Attorney’s office declined at the time to review additional evidence, including more interviews gathered by the campus police department, beyond a six-page statement signed by Doe, according to records obtained by The New York Times . Prosecutors did not express interest in the additional evidence because they had decided, based on Doe’s statement, that “criminal charges would not be pursued in this case,” a Cornell police investigator wrote in a note documenting the call, according to the Times.
Help is available : For help in the US, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-467

articles.title_orig: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.title_zh: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.content_orig:
Credit : Bryce Richter / UW–Madison
An astrophysics column on big questions and our universe.
There’s a whole entire Universe out there, and the more we learn about it as it actually is, the greater our potential becomes to achieve great things as a civilization, even if the path from knowledge to improving humanity is far from clear. The Nobel Prize was set up more than 100 years ago with the express purpose of rewarding those whose work provides the “greatest benefit to humankind” in a number of disciplines, including physics. We couldn’t foresee that:
Similarly, we cannot know what advances will arise in the future from advances made today in fields like elementary particle physics, gravitational waves, or neutrino astronomy, but possibilities range from computational advances to superior timekeeping technologies to extraterrestrial communication. One thing is certain, however: we have to make the fundamental advance, first, if we ever hope to find out. In many ways, that’s what the science of physics is all about.
It’s for that reason that the world ought to be incredibly excited that the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics has gone to Francis Halzen , for “decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” which is a remarkable testament to what a single individual can accomplish with a creative idea, a lot of hard work and organization, persistence, a strong national investment in science, and quite a bit of good luck. Here’s the story of this remarkable advance in neutrino physics and astrophysics.
The idea of IceCube was born 39 years ago, back before “neutrino astrophysics” was a field that went beyond our Solar System. Prior to 1987, neutrino astrophysics was restricted solely to measuring the neutrinos coming from within the Solar System: by building a large tank of fluid deep underground. Starting in 1968 , the idea was that neutrinos from the Sun, occasionally, would interact with an atomic nucleus, transmuting a neutron into a proton, and converting the neutrino into an electron in the process. By looking for the newly transmuted nuclei, solar neutrinos could then be detected.
In principle, nuclear reactions would occur all across the Universe, releasing neutrinos when they did, but the flux would be far too low to detect them. However, due to contemporaneous interest in grand unified theories , particle physicists had begun building much larger tanks of fluid surrounded by photomultiplier tubes, with the idea being to detect any spontaneously decaying protons by measuring their faster-than-light in the liquid medium radiation: Cherenkov radiation .
The major experiment of the 1980s, Kamiokande , was originally an experiment to search for nucleon decay in Kamioka, Japan. Running for several years, it only obtained null results, until the day of February 24, 1987. All of a sudden, an array of signals emerged: 12 of them (antineutrinos, technically) in the Kamiokande II detector alone . Four hours later, the light arrived as well, confirming this was indeed a supernova event. Kamiokande, the Kamioka nucleon decay experiment, kept the same acronym, but renamed itself to the Kamioka neutrino detector experiment. From a failed search for proton decay , the science of neutrino astronomy was born.
Over the subsequent years and decades, most approaches to neutrino detection simply scaled up this approach. Large, underground, liquid-filled detectors lined with photomultiplier tubes optimized to detect Cherenkov radiation were the key to building neutrino detectors, including Super-Kamiokande and the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNOLab), where the original research led to a Nobel Prize awarded in 2002 for neutrino physics and the upgraded research led to one in 2015 for neutrino oscillations.
However, in the aftermath of the 1987 supernova and subsequent neutrino detection, Francis Halzen began thinking about a different approach. Giant tanks were fundamentally limited in a key way: the effective volume available for interactions with neutrinos was constrained to be no larger than the size of your tank. If you wanted to find rare events, your only options were to either build a larger tank or to wait for longer periods of time, until such a neutrino from a rare event happened to interact within your detector.
Halzen came up with an alternative in 1988, which he merely (and humbly) referred to as a “cute idea,” which was to do away with a photomultiplier tube-lined tank entirely. Instead, he wondered, given that there’s so much ice located at the Earth’s south pole, could one simply use Antarctic ice as the “detector” for interacting with neutrinos instead?
Of course, it wouldn’t be possible or practical to use the entire Antarctic ice sheet, but Halzen realized that if you restricted yourself to a mere section of it — a large, cubical block — you could vastly increase the potential interaction volume over what you could ever hope to build with a conventional, liquid-filled and photomultiplier tube-lined detector. If it could be implemented successfully, Halzen’s vision could bring about a neutrino detector that was able to see events that were far rarer than the other neutrino detector designs would be sensitive to.
We had a longstanding hint of this from cosmic rays: non-neutrino particles (mostly protons, but also some heavier nuclei) that struck and interacted with Earth’s upper atmosphere, producing energetic particle showers. Sometimes, the daughter particles emerging from the shower could be detected directly on the ground, but most frequently, the shower of particles would interact with the Earth’s atmosphere: moving faster-than-light in the medium of air, and producing a cone of blue light that was once again the hallmark of Cherenkov radiation. Arrays of Cherenkov telescopes routinely detect this light, and reconstruct the signatures (and energies) of the particles that originally created them. When they do, they find that there are cosmic particles out there far, far more energetic than anything we could ever hope to realistically produce in laboratory experiments here on Earth.
If these high-energy particles — albeit, rare particles — are out there in the Universe, ostensibly created by high-energy sources like neutron stars, black holes, and active quasars, then it stands to reason that similar processes will create ultra-energetic neutrinos as well. However, since the number of particles above a given energy rapidly decreases as a function of energy, it would also imply that ultra high-energy neutrino events should be exceedingly rare as well, requiring enormous volumes of “detector material” in order to even see one or a few of them.
Super-Kamiokande is the world’s largest operational neutrino detector tank, holding just over 50,000 tonnes of extraordinarily pure water, but is only about 40 meters on a side. (Technically, in a cylindrical shape.) For comparison, however, if you went deep into the Antarctic ice, you should be able to find ice that is:
Halzen’s idea was to use hot water to bore cylindrical holes straight down into the Antarctic ice at regularly spaced intervals, and then to place specialized Cherenkov detectors down deep within the ice itself, filling the gaps back up with water to restore the ice back to its pristine, block-like state. If these detectors were spaced out over a volume of ice that was a cubic kilometer in size — 1 km × 1 km × 1 km — it would possess 20,000 times the detection volume of Super-Kamiokande!
The prototype for what would become the IceCube neutrino detector was known as AMANDA: the Antarctic Muon And Neutrino Detector Array . AMANDA was made up of optical modules — each with one photomultiplier tube inside to be sensitive to Cherenkov light — that were sunk into the Antarctic ice beneath the Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station. articles.title_orig: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.title_zh: Doja Cat’s ‘Tour Ma Vie World Tour’ tests her performer bona fides
articles.content_orig:
When an artist abandons the standard fanfare and extravagance of an arena tour, their true performance ability is put to the test. Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” demonstrated her showmanship needs no hefty entourage of backup dancers, elaborate sets or choreography.
The tour, which hit Chicago’s United Center on Oct. 3, traverses the R&B artist’s ’80s-infused 2025 album “Vie,” while incorporating older hits like “Need to Know” and “Say So.” Apart from a handful of male backup dancers and occasional pyrotechnics, her tour is largely an understated affair as she commands the audience’s attention almost entirely on her own.
Opening with a hearty brass interlude, Doja Cat began the evening with “Cards,” the first track on “Vie.” Her performance evoked sartorial themes of the ’80s, as she donned pink geometric yoga pants and a bright orange cheetah-patterned coat. Vibrant lighting punctuated the disco-heavy setlist as Doja Cat ventured further into the album, which combines dance-pop and disco.
Her newest album and its accompanying tour are quite a departure for Doja Cat, whose earlier discography is primarily contemporary R&B and rap.
While the show’s runtime focused heavily on “Vie,” Doja Cat gained substantial mileage from older hits like “Need to Know” from her 2021 album “Planet Her” and “Streets” from her 2019 album “Hot Pink,” a testament to her artistic depth.
The concert presents Doja Cat at her most comfortable, highlighting the signature unseriousness that makes her such a compelling performer. At one point, she playfully lit a cigarette before jumping back into song. Later on, she pied an audience member in the face during a tongue-in-cheek interactive skit.
Though there were scattered moments of grandeur, Doja Cat was at her best when she was alone onstage, commanding the audience without flashy costume changes or theatrical gimmicks.
The most memorable track from the evening was unequivocally “Paint The Town Red,” a hit from her 2023 album “Scarlet.” Unaccompanied by background vocals, Doja Cat exerted a larger-than-life stage presence throughout the track, eliciting deafening cheers from the audience.
True to form, Doja Cat concluded the concert on a high note, launching a pyrotechnics show to close out the night and putting her band centerstage for an epic guitar solo. Bouncing between fan favorites like “Tia Tamera” and new songs like “Stranger,” the artist underscored her thematic versatility as a performer.
Though her performance was notably unostentatious, Doja Cat’s “Tour Ma Vie World Tour” proves she is a born performer. With a refined yet metamorphic style, Doja Cat demonstrated she can be as dynamic as she is iconic.

articles.title_orig: FlyDubai Attacker Was Part of Pilot Hiring Spree at Fast-Growing Airline
articles.title_zh: FlyDubai Attacker Was Part of Pilot Hiring Spree at Fast-Growing Airline
articles.content_orig:
The alleged hijacker of the Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv likely wanted to target Israel’s Ben Gurion Airport, the country’s main international gateway, according to an Israeli official and an Israeli source familiar with the matter.
Hamam al-Hammami, the suspect in the hijacking attempt and co-pilot on board the flight, was stopped by the actions of the captain and several passengers who restrained him and wrested control of the airplane.
The official and the source said Israel is receiving updates from the Emiratis and that the investigation was still in its early stages. There are still questions about the suspect’s intentions, they added.
Israel’s Channel 12 News first reported that Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport may have been the target of the hijacking.
It’s unclear why al-Hammami allegedly attacked the captain, Smit Machchhar, over Saudi airspace if his goal was to target an airport in Israel. When Israel detected an inbound commercial jet signaling a potential hijacking on September 30, authorities there scrambled Israeli fighter jets as a precaution – standard procedure for such an emergency scenario.
The United Arab Emirates is leading the investigation into the attempted hijacking on board Flydubai’s FZ1073 to learn the motives behind the attack and understand how the suspect was able to get through the safeguards of two countries known for their strict security protocols.
Israel’s Tax Authority confirmed the names of all passengers and crew were in the hands of Israeli authorities before the flight had taken off, but it said questions about the vetting of crew members should be referred to the Ministry of Transport. Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security agency, also referred CNN to the Ministry of Transport, which it said is “responsible for all security matters concerning foreign airlines.”
The Ministry of Transport said that its procedures do not include checking the names of flight crew members, although those names are submitted to the Israel Tax Authority, which collects them in case of requests by security services.
The ministry added that all flight crew members are required to have a travel visa to enter the country, and an Omani passport should have been flagged at check-in. But the ministry also said its “procedures do not address the threat from a pilot.”
CNN reported on Sunday that the suspect probably acted alone , and Israel is so far not aware of a link to any terrorist organization that trained, funded, or organized the attack.
The attorney general of the UAE, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said the co-pilot on board the flight had attempted to seize control of the plane by attacking his colleague with a crash ax – a piece of equipment required on most aircraft. The attorney general called the attempted hijacking a “terrorist act.”
The suspect, al-Hammami, had been removed from his previous job at Oman’s national airline on the track to be a pilot following concerns about his extremist views, sources told CNN earlier. He was moved to a desk job at the company, one of the sources said.
Flydubai said it couldn’t comment on the matter while an investigation was underway. CNN has also reached out to Oman Air, the UAE Foreign Ministry and the Dubai government’s media office for comment.
Aviation experts have told CNN that when it comes to vetting pilots, the responsibility lies with local governments, airlines and security services. Experts said pilots’ licenses and security passes are handled at the national level, and the rules vary depending on the country.
CNN’s Kylie Atwood contributed reporting.

Jaguar has unveiled Type 01, the most technologically advanced and powerful Jaguar in the brand’s history.
New York, USA, 6 October 2026: Jaguar has unveiled Type 01, the most technologically advanced and powerful Jaguar in the brand’s history. A luxury four‑door GT that never arrives unnoticed.
Type 01 inspired a celebration of contemporary culture across New York. This was a one‑of‑a‑kind premiere, from large‑scale digital displays in Times Square, DUMBO and the Lower East Side, to its dynamic arrival for an exclusive gathering at STORIED in West Chelsea, zip code 10001.
Type 01 is defined by exuberant proportions, with its low roofline, long bonnet, sleek silhouette and dramatic presence. Starting from a single line and a blank sheet of paper, it is the most aerodynamic and powerful Jaguar road car. A bold, one‑of‑a‑kind that breaks convention, with a clear lineage to the great Jaguars of the past including the E‑type and XJS.
Beneath Type 01’s clean surfaces is a bespoke Jaguar Electric Architecture which offers more than 1,000PS, always with power in reserve, for a drive that is unmistakably Jaguar. Powered by an 850‑volt electrical architecture, it delivers a 400‑mile range (EPA) and adds 200 miles in 13 minutes using 350kW charging. Type 01 represents a new standard of power, aerodynamics and technological advancement for Jaguar.
From its dramatic design to its captivating drive, Type 01 distils the essence of Jaguar into a luxury grand tourer for a new era. Type 01 is the foundation of this British brand, one that makes no compromise between design and engineering in our quest to create objects of desire, just as it was in the days of the E‑type and XJS.
At the world premiere of Type 01 at STORIED in New York, Jaguar announced acclaimed actor Florence Pugh as the inaugural brand ambassador for its new era. Embodying the originality, fearlessness and creative spirit that define Jaguar.
Pugh joined guests and friends of the brand to celebrate the global arrival of Type 01 with a night dedicated to bold creativity and artistic expression. British singer‑songwriter Sienna Spiro, Best New Artist at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards, performed an intimate set. Celebrated chef Roze Traoré conceived an exclusive culinary programme inspired by Jaguar's fearless creative vision.
New York provided the brand with an international stage from which to celebrate originality and British innovation – a city where art, fashion, film, music and design create one of the world’s most influential centres of reinvention.
At STORIED NYC, guests encountered a series of product artefacts exploring the artistry that brought the Type 01 vision to life:
The STORIED reveal sequence began with Type 01’s dynamic arrival, driven by António Félix da Costa from the World Championship‑winning Jaguar TCS Racing team.
This was the biggest moment since the Jaguar name was born in 1935. A fitting tribute and a powerful expression of Jaguar's dramatic new era. A new chapter for the brand begins with Type 01. Jaguar is back. Orders open early 2027 with first client deliveries expected in the second half of the year. Prices start from 130,000 GBP.

A luxury four‑door GT, Type 01 embodies Jaguar's renewed vision of modern luxury, combining dramatic design, craftsmanship and innovation to create an unmistakable presence and emotional connection.

By Charity L. Cohen / 10/06/2026 Alumni , College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences
EAST GREENSBORO, N.C. (Oct. 6, 2026) – Forever a North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University Aggie and now a Hillman College Falcon, former Mister A&T Joshua Suiter ‘22 is starring in the Netflix reboot of the 1980s and 1990s hit sitcom “A Different World.”
The series, which debuted at No. 1 on Netflix in the U.S., has already been renewed for a second season. It builds on the cultural impact of the original series, which helped shape national perceptions of historically Black college and university (HBCU) life and inspired generations of students.
Following a new generation of students at the iconic fictional HBCU, Hillman College, the sequel explores the lives of today’s students while examining the legacy of those who came before them. The series’ writing team includes Ashley Laverne Jackson, daughter of late civil rights leader the Rev. Jesse Jackson ‘64.
Suiter portrays Andre, a fellow Hillman student alongside Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), daughter of original characters Whitley (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne (Kadeem Hardison). As Deborah begins her journey at Hillman, she works to establish her own identity beyond her parents’ legacy while experiencing the highs and challenges of campus life.
“Seeing all the love for Andre really hit home,” Suiter said. “He’s one of my favorite characters thus far, and we created him from scratch, so to know that the hard work is being received and folks want more encourages me to keep going.”
Suiter discovered his calling for acting and musical theater at 7, quickly realizing that hours spent studying lines and practicing techniques felt like minutes. That passion led him to N.C. A&T, where he earned a B.F.A. in professional theatre from the College of Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences.
While at A&T, Suiter built a strong foundation in the performing arts, gaining experience both on stage and behind the scenes. One of his notable performances was in “Ain’t Misbehavin’” during the university’s first Town & Gown Gala in 2019, where he first met Guy, who reprises her role as Whitley in the reboot.
In addition to acting, Suiter worked as a theater technician and developed skills in the marketing and business aspects of performance and the entertainment industry. This versatility helped propel him into his professional career.
“I came in as a creative, but what A&T did between Alpha Phi Alpha, the classes, talking business with professors and serving as Mister A&T sharpened me on the business side,” said Suiter. “It sharpened my networking skills while showing me how to be authentic to who I am.”
As a talented and emerging actor who most recently appeared in the Hulu series “All’s Fair,” performing alongside prominent Hollywood actors, starring in “A Different World” represents a full-circle moment for Suiter as an HBCU alumnus, bringing him into a reimagined version of a series he grew up watching.
“When you talk about an HBCU experience, I’m putting mine up there with the best of them,” he said. “I have so many experiences to pull from with the run of this show, with the character Andre. Hillman even has a heartbeat of its own, so it’s been fun exploring what that feels like as a student there, while still carrying that Aggie Pride in my heart.”
